title: Bind Key
description: Declare that the issuer uses a cryptographic key that is not directly managed by its KEL (e.g. to conform to an external standard). Issuing this ACDC makes the key binding provable and revocable.
$comment: These credentials are intentionally public and untargeted. They lack an issuee, they carry no privacy nonce, and they do not support compaction: the announcement IS the content, so a form with the key withheld would say nothing.

t.description: Message type. Optional; an ACDC JSON message without it is of type acm.

i.description: AID of the issuer declaring the key binding

rd.description: SAID of the registry whose TEL carries this credential's issuance and revocation. Required: a key binding that cannot be revoked is a claim nobody can withdraw, and revocability is half of what this credential exists to provide.

a.description: Attributes block. Uncompactable by design: this credential is a public announcement, so there is no form of it worth presenting with the key withheld.

dt.description: When the issuer made this declaration, as an ISO-8601 datetime

pubkey.description: The public key the issuer declares it uses, encoded as keyFormat says. No pattern is asserted here: the encodings this field admits are checked by whoever parses the key, and a pattern this repo cannot test against a real issuer of each format would reject legitimate keys (the lesson the privacy nonce taught in @4t5t4yca).

keyFormat.description: How pubkey is encoded. Required rather than defaulted: a JSON Schema default is an annotation nothing applies, so an absent keyFormat would leave two readers free to parse the same key differently.

validFrom.description: When the issuer intends the binding to start, as an ISO-8601 datetime. Absent means it starts on issuance.

validUntil.description: When the issuer intends the binding to stop, as an ISO-8601 datetime. Absent means the issuer set no horizon, so the binding stops only on revocation — never that it is perpetual.

uses.description: Short strings naming the ways the issuer intends to use this key. Declarative only: a verifier gets no authority from them that its own governance did not already grant.

items.$comment: Enum omitted to stay flexible, but use these examples where they apply.

oneOf.const: The issuer declares that it uses this key. It does not assert that the key is uncompromised, well managed, generated soundly, or held only by the issuer, and a verifier MUST NOT read any of those into this credential.

l.const: The issuer declares that it uses this key. It does not assert that the key is uncompromised, well managed, generated soundly, or held only by the issuer, and a verifier MUST NOT read any of those into this credential.

oneOf.const: The uses field says what the issuer intends the key for. It confers no authority and creates no obligation on anyone: a verifier that treats a declared use as permission has granted that permission itself.

l.const: The uses field says what the issuer intends the key for. It confers no authority and creates no obligation on anyone: a verifier that treats a declared use as permission has granted that permission itself.

oneOf.const: The binding holds from validFrom, or from issuance when none is stated, until validUntil or revocation, whichever comes first. An absent validUntil means the issuer set no horizon, never that the binding is perpetual, and a verifier MUST check the registry before relying on one.

l.const: The binding holds from validFrom, or from issuance when none is stated, until validUntil or revocation, whichever comes first. An absent validUntil means the issuer set no horizon, never that the binding is perpetual, and a verifier MUST check the registry before relying on one.

oneOf.const: A verifier that does not recognize a credential's keyFormat MUST refuse to use the key rather than guess at its encoding. A later version of this schema may name a format this one does not, and a key parsed under the wrong assumption is worse than a key not parsed at all.

l.const: A verifier that does not recognize a credential's keyFormat MUST refuse to use the key rather than guess at its encoding. A later version of this schema may name a format this one does not, and a key parsed under the wrong assumption is worse than a key not parsed at all.
